app.title: CurveCurator dashboard: explore fitted dose-response curves on a volcano or potency plot
app.summary: A person opens a dashboard of dose-response curves that have already been fitted and tested for significance. Every curve is a dot on a volcano plot (fold change against p-value or relevance score) or on a potency plot (fold change against pEC50), with the significance boundary drawn in. They narrow the dots by regulation class, by pEC50, score and signal range sliders, and by regex search on names, sequences or genes. Then they select curves by clicking, lassoing or searching to see the measured points and fitted sigmoid, where each curve falls in the potency, signal and score distributions, and its fit statistics in a sortable table. What they get is a set of hit curves they have checked, which they can save as figures.

task.text: Find the curves with a significant, relevant dose response among many fitted curves, and check each one's fit and potency.

data.text: A table of fitted dose-response curves: one row per sample or analyte, with response ratios at each dose and fitted parameters (pEC50, slope, front, back), fold change, p-value, relevance score, AUC, R², signal quality and regulation class.
data.item: one fitted dose-response curve for one sample or analyte

stage.text: exploring fitted dose-response curves after the fitting and significance run, to pick out and check hits

mechanism.text: A volcano or potency scatter of every curve drives the other views: selecting dots by tap, lasso or regex search draws their measured points and fitted sigmoids in the curve panel, marks them in the pEC50, signal and score histograms, and lists them in the table. The regulation toggle and range sliders hide dots that fail the filters and move the threshold lines on the histograms.

field.text: dose-response curve fitting with significance thresholding in pharmacology

workflow.name: screen many fitted curves for significant hits and inspect each one

steps.step: look over every item at a glance
steps.here: every fitted curve is a dot on the volcano plot (log2 curve fold change against -log10 p-value), coloured by pEC50, with the red decision boundary drawn from alpha and the fold-change limit

steps.step: switch which statistic the overview shows
steps.here: a Volcano/Potency dropdown changes the y-axis to pEC50; p-value/Relevance (or adjusted p-value) buttons switch the significance axis and its threshold line

steps.step: filter to the items that matter
steps.here: all/regulated/not-regulated buttons plus pEC50, Score and Signal range sliders hide curves outside the limits; dashed threshold lines move on the matching histograms

steps.step: find items by name or pattern
steps.here: regex search boxes for Name, Modified sequence and Gene, with an optional case-sensitive checkbox, select every visible curve whose field matches

tapping, shift-clicking or lassoing dots draws each selected curve's measured ratios and fitted 4-parameter sigmoid against log concentration, and puts a red line where it falls in the pEC50, signal and score histograms

steps.step: read and sort the values of the selected items
steps.here: the table lists only the selected curves, with pEC50, slope, fold change, AUC, R², relevance and signal quality; headers sort and a row click narrows the selection
each plot's save tool writes the current view out as a PNG or SVG figure

distinctive: significance is judged in two dimensions at once: a curved boundary over fold change and p-value (SAM-style s0 relevance score) instead of a single p-value cutoff
the potency view shows only significant curves by default, because pEC50 is only meaningful for regulated curves
the sigmoid is redrawn in the browser from each curve's stored pEC50, slope, front and back, over a log-dose axis padded half a decade beyond the tested doses
the histograms beside the curve panel place each selected curve within the distributions of potency, control signal and identification score
searches take regular expressions, so a sequence motif can select every matching analyte at once
